blocks.content: Mizoram's demography chapter centres on three exceptional superlatives — an overwhelming Scheduled Tribe population share, one of India's highest literacy rates, and a very high Christian population share — each a frequently tested comparative fact.

cells: approx 10.97 lakh (1.097 million) — one of India's least populous states
approx 94-95% — among the highest of any Indian state
approx 87% — one of the highest Christian population shares of any Indian state
approx 91-92% — among the highest of any Indian state, second only to Kerala in several recent rankings

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Mizoram's literacy rate (~91-92%) is consistently ranked among the very highest of any Indian state, frequently cited as second only to Kerala — a frequently tested superlative alongside its very high ST (~94-95%) and Christian (~87%) population shares.

items: The Mizo people (Chapter 2) form the overwhelming majority of the state's population, comprising numerous historically distinct clans/sub-tribes (including Lusei/Lushai, Hmar, Paite, Ralte, and others) that have, over time, developed a substantially unified modern Mizo identity, particularly following the spread of Christianity and a common Duhlian-based Mizo literary language (below).

Smaller distinct tribal communities — notably the Chakma, Mara (Lakher) and Lai (Pawi), each with its own Sixth Schedule Autonomous District Council (Chapter 5) — maintain more clearly distinct ethnic, linguistic and cultural identities from the wider Mizo community, concentrated in specific border areas of the state.

The Chakma community is notably distinct from most other communities covered in this book in one key respect: many Chakma in Mizoram (and neighbouring states) are Buddhist, whereas the wider Mizo and other main communities of the state are overwhelmingly Christian — a religious-demographic exception worth noting.

blocks.content: Christianity was introduced to the Mizo Hills by Welsh Calvinist Methodist and Baptist missionaries from the late 19th century onward (following British annexation, Chapter 2), leading over subsequent decades to near-total conversion of the Mizo population — a transformation broadly comparable in scale and pace to Nagaland's and Meghalaya's own Christian-conversion histories.

The Presbyterian Church (Mizoram Synod) and the Baptist Church of Mizoram are the two largest denominations, and Christian churches continue to hold significant social, cultural and (informally) political influence in Mizoram's public life — including active roles in social reform campaigns (notably anti-alcohol and anti-drug advocacy) and community welfare activities.

items: Mizo (Duhlian, based primarily on the Lusei/Lushai dialect) is the official language of the state and serves as a common literary and administrative language uniting the various Mizo clan dialects, belonging to the Kuki-Chin-Mizo (Zo) branch of the Tibeto-Burman language family — the same broader language family as the Kuki-Zo languages of Manipur (companion volume) and the Chin languages of Myanmar.
English is widely used alongside Mizo in education, administration and official contexts, reflecting the strong historical influence of Christian missionary education.
Population (2011): approx 10.97 lakh; ST share approx 94-95%; Christian share approx 87%; literacy approx 91-92% (2nd highest after Kerala in several rankings).
Mizo = a unified modern identity encompassing Lusei/Lushai, Hmar, Paite, Ralte and other clans; smaller distinct communities (Chakma, Mara, Lai) have their own Sixth Schedule ADCs.
Chakma community is notably Buddhist, distinct from the overwhelmingly Christian Mizo majority.
Presbyterian Church (Mizoram Synod) and Baptist Church of Mizoram are the two largest denominations; churches hold significant social/cultural influence.
Mizo (Duhlian) = official language, Kuki-Chin-Mizo (Zo) branch of Tibeto-Burman, same broader family as Manipur's Kuki-Zo languages.
